answers.answer:
NAD(P) binding has arisen in several unrelated protein architectures, and SCOPe 2.08 reflects this. Examples: c.2.1 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains' (fold c.2, a 3-layer a/b/a Rossmann-like fold, which includes the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase and related families); c.3.1 'FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain' (fold c.3, a different Rossmann-like fold that also binds FAD); and c.1.7 'NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductase' (the aldo-keto reductase superfamily, in the TIM-barrel fold c.1). All three are in class c (a/b), but they sit in different folds and superfamilies. The same cofactor therefore has no single evolutionary origin.

What this implies:
- Divergent evolution (homology) is a claim about shared ancestry. SCOPe supports it inside a superfamily, where structure, conserved sequence motifs and often function indicate common descent. Within c.2.1, for example, the shared dinucleotide-binding Rossmann core is good evidence of common ancestry for those families.
- Between different folds or superfamilies (c.2.1 versus c.1.7, say), the NAD(P) binding is better read as convergent evolution, or at least as not demonstrably homologous. The chemistry of NAD(P) redox is useful, so different scaffolds have independently evolved ways to bind it. Even where the Rossmann-like folds c.2 and c.3 look alike, SCOPe keeps them as separate folds and superfamilies. Their similarity may be an ancient common origin, or it may come from shared structural constraints on a mononucleotide/dinucleotide-binding a/b motif. The evidence is not strong enough to call them homologous at superfamily level.
- So 'NAD(P)-binding' is a functional or ligand category, not an evolutionary one. Class, fold, superfamily and family in SCOPe are different strengths of evidence. Family means clear homology, usually with detectable sequence similarity or very similar structure and function. Superfamily means probable common ancestry from structure and function even with low sequence identity. Fold means only a similar arrangement and topology of secondary structure, with no claim of homology. Class means only the broad secondary-structure composition.

Why cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is insufficient:
- Convergence. Unrelated scaffolds can arrive independently at a similar pocket, catalytic geometry or residue arrangement. Typical cases are a Tyr-Lys catalytic pair, nucleotide-binding loops, or a nicotinamide stacking site. Matching local active-site residues, such as a catalytic triad, is classic analogy rather than homology.
- The same ligand imposes the same physical constraints (hydrogen bonding to the pyrophosphate and ribose, hydrophobic stacking of the nicotinamide), which produces similar local motifs even without ancestry.
- Binding is a small part of the structure. Homology needs the overall fold, its topology and the connectivity of secondary-structure elements, backed by sequence, conserved motifs and domain architecture. Ligand contacts alone do not show this.
- Divergent evolution can also change function or cofactor. Homologous proteins may bind different cofactors (for example NAD versus NADP, or FAD, or none), so cofactor identity does not define the evolutionary boundary in either direction.
- Limits on transfer. Do not infer homology from a shared cofactor, do not transfer function or catalytic mechanism across folds or superfamilies, and do not choose templates or representatives by cofactor alone. Use a template only when the SCOPe fold, superfamily or family relationship and sequence or structure alignment support it. Within a superfamily, even homologous members can have different substrates and specificity, so use family-level evidence for function transfer.
- Practical rule: treat NAD(P)-binding as a functional annotation. Assign evolutionary relationships from SCOPe hierarchy placement, structure and sequence evidence, and expert curation, and do not use cofactor presence to merge folds or superfamilies.
